cmimc-2021-geometry-d2-01.title: Rhombi
cmimc-2021-geometry-d2-01.body:
$BC=\sqrt{20^2+21^2}=29$ and, since $A$ is a right angle, $AM=BM=CM=\frac{29}2$. The circles $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ both have radius $\frac{29}2$ ($AM=BM$), so their intersection points $M$ and $X$ are reflections of each other across the line of centres $AB$. Thus $XA=XB=BM=AM$ and $AMBX$ is a rhombus; similarly $AMCY$ is a rhombus of the same side length. Hence $XB\parallel AM\parallel CY$ and $XB=AM=CY$, so $XBCY$ is a parallelogram and $XY=BC=29$.

**Answer: 29**

cmimc-2021-geometry-d2-03.title: Extend the legs
cmimc-2021-geometry-d2-03.body:
Extend $DA$ and $CB$ to meet at $E$. In $\triangle DEC$, $\angle D+\angle C=90^\circ$, so $\angle DEC=90^\circ$ and $\angle AEB=90^\circ$. The midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is its circumcentre, so $EM_2=\frac{CD}2=\frac92$ and $EM_1=\frac{AB}2=\frac52$. Because $AB\parallel CD$, the triangles $EAB$ and $EDC$ are similar with $E,M_1,M_2$ collinear, so $M_1M_2=EM_2-EM_1=\frac92-\frac52=2$.

(Alternatively, for any trapezoid with $\angle C+\angle D=90^\circ$, the segment joining the midpoints of the parallel sides equals half the difference of the bases.)

**Answer: 2**

cmimc-2021-geometry-d2-04.title: Cross-sections perpendicular to the diagonal
cmimc-2021-geometry-d2-04.body:
The diagonal has length $\sqrt{20+80}=10$. The feet of the perpendiculars from the other two vertices divide it into pieces $\frac{(2\sqrt5)^2}{10}=2$ and $\frac{(4\sqrt5)^2}{10}=8$, and these vertices are at distance $\frac{2\sqrt5\cdot4\sqrt5}{10}=4$ from the diagonal. Place the diagonal on the $t$-axis, $0\le t\le10$. On one side of it the rectangle reaches distance $r_1(t)=2t$ for $t\le2$ and $\frac{10-t}2$ for $t\ge2$; on the other side $r_2(t)=\frac t2$ for $t\le8$ and $2(10-t)$ for $t\ge8$.

At height $t$, rotating by $\theta$ sweeps, at distance $r\le r_1$ an arc of angle $\theta$ on one side and, at distance $r\le r_2$, an arc of angle $\theta$ on the opposite side (shifted by $\pi$). Let $\rho_{\min}=\min(r_1,r_2)$ and $\rho_{\max}=\max(r_1,r_2)$.

- For $\theta\le\pi$ the two arcs never overlap, so the swept area at height $t$ is $\frac\theta2(r_1^2+r_2^2)$ and $V(\theta)=\frac\theta2\int_0^{10}(r_1^2+r_2^2)\,dt=\frac\theta2\cdot\frac{320}{3}=\frac{160\theta}{3}$.
- For $\pi\le\theta\le2\pi$ the two arcs together cover the full circle out to radius $\rho_{\min}$, and only an arc of angle $\theta$ between $\rho_{\min}$ and $\rho_{\max}$. So $V(\theta)=\pi\int\rho_{\min}^2\,dt+\frac\theta2\int(\rho_{\max}^2-\rho_{\min}^2)\,dt$. The two profiles cross at $t=5$; computing the integrals gives $\int\rho_{\min}^2\,dt=\frac{125}6$ and $\int\rho_{\max}^2\,dt=\frac{515}6$, so $V(\theta)=\frac{125\pi}{6}+\frac{65}{2}\theta$.

Since $V(\pi)=\frac{160\pi}3<62\pi$, the angle exceeds $\pi$. Solving $\frac{125\pi}6+\frac{65}2\theta=62\pi$ gives $\theta=\frac{247\pi}{195}=\frac{19\pi}{15}$, i.e. $228^\circ$. (A direct numerical integration of the swept volume at $228^\circ$ gives $62\pi$.)

**Answer: 228 degrees**

cmimc-2021-geometry-d2-05.title: Describe the reachable region
cmimc-2021-geometry-d2-05.body:
Let $E=(0,0)$, $S=(1,0)$ (spider), $H=(2+\sqrt2,0)$ (home). Emily's distance to $S$ only increases from $1$ and her distance to $H$ only decreases from $2+\sqrt2$, so she always stays

1. outside the unit circle about $S$ (distance to $S$ is at least $1$),
2. inside the circle about $H$ of radius $2+\sqrt2$,
3. inside the circle about $S$ of radius $1+\sqrt2$ (her final distance to $S$ is $HS=1+\sqrt2$, and distance to $S$ never decreases).

Circles (2) and (3) meet at $A=(1,1+\sqrt2)$ and $B=(1,-(1+\sqrt2))$, with $AS\perp EH$. One checks that every point of the resulting region can indeed be visited: to the left of line $AB$ Emily walks along a circle centred on $SH$ through $E$, then goes right and follows the boundary home; to the right of $AB$ she first reaches the left boundary of that part and then walks right, then follows the boundary.

**Area.** Right of line $AB$ (the line $x=1$): half of the disc about $S$ of radius $1+\sqrt2$, area $\frac\pi2(1+\sqrt2)^2$. Left of $AB$: the part of the disc about $H$ of radius $2+\sqrt2$, which is a quarter disc (since $\angle AHB=90^\circ$) minus triangle $ABH$: $\frac\pi4(2+\sqrt2)^2-\frac12(2+\sqrt2)^2$. Then remove the unit disc about $S$ (area $\pi$):
$$\frac\pi2(3+2\sqrt2)+\frac\pi4(6+4\sqrt2)-\frac12(6+4\sqrt2)-\pi=(2+2\sqrt2)\pi-3-2\sqrt2.$$

**Answer: $(2+2\sqrt2)\pi-3-2\sqrt2$**
